text:
This research analyzes best practices and new configuration directives for OpenSSH client (ssh_config) as of July 2026. Key areas of focus include post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transition, connection activity management using modern directives, and client protection against statistical network traffic analysis.

Default Post-Quantum Transition: Beginning with OpenSSH 10.0, the hybrid key exchange algorithm mlkem768x25519-sha256 became default, providing quantum resistance over classical curve25519-sha256 [1]. OpenSSH 10.4 added experimental support for composite digital signatures mldsa44-ed25519 [4].
Weak Cryptography Guardrails: The WarnWeakCrypto directive in version 10.1 enables interactive warnings when non-post-quantum algorithms are negotiated, addressing Store-Now-Decrypt-Later (SNDL) risks [2], [10].
Granular Channel Timeouts: ChannelTimeout enables independent inactivity termination across channel types (X11, TCP forwarding, interactive sessions), replacing inefficient keep-alive polling [5], [9].
Timing Attack Defenses: ObscureKeystrokeTiming masks keystroke timing patterns using 20ms quantization and decoy chaff packets [1], [5].

Primary Recommendation: Engineers must configure ssh_config with hybrid key exchange priority mlkem768x25519-sha256, enforce host key auditing via DNSSEC/SSHFP, declare granular timeouts using ChannelTimeout, and enable WarnWeakCrypto for session auditing [1], [2], [5].
Confidence Level: High. The study relies on official OpenSSH release notes (10.0-10.4), NIST FIPS 203/204 standards, and practical configuration syntax audits on local workstations.
Assumption 2 (Hardware-Backed Tokens): Authentication utilizes FIDO2 Security Keys or GnuPG smartcard agent routing (YubiKey / Secure Enclave), preventing unencrypted private key storage on disk.
Assumption 3 (Local Client): Local macOS workstation runs OpenSSH 10.0+, enabling Match version syntax.

Key Evidence: OpenSSH 10.0 enables hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256 by default [1]. WarnWeakCrypto in OpenSSH 10.1 alerts on non-PQC connections [2]. NIST FIPS 203 defines Module Learning with Errors (M-LWE) mathematical hardness [6].

Implications: Declaring mlkem768x25519-sha256 and sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com in KexAlgorithms provides post-quantum payload protection. WarnWeakCrypto yes alerts operators when falling back to legacy servers.

While post-quantum key exchange (KEX) is standardized and active by default, post-quantum digital signatures for host and user authentication are experimental. OpenSSH 10.4 introduced experimental composite signature mldsa44-ed25519 [4] combining NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA [7] and Ed25519. Unrecognized algorithm tokens cause fatal parser termination on OpenSSH < 10.4 [4], [5].

Key Evidence: OpenSSH 10.4 requires explicit configuration in HostKeyAlgorithms and PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms to use mldsa44-ed25519 [4]. On OpenSSH 10.2p1, declaring mldsa44-ed25519 causes fatal parser failure 'Bad key types' [5].
NIST FIPS 204 standardizes ML-DSA based on Crystals-Dilithium lattices, providing high performance and compact signature size [7].

Implications: Configuration files must keep experimental mldsa44-ed25519 algorithms commented or scoped until client binaries are upgraded globally to 10.4+, keeping proven algorithms like ssh-ed25519 active.

Connection lifecycle management evolved with the introduction of ChannelTimeout and UnusedConnectionTimeout in OpenSSH 9.2 [9]. ChannelTimeout sets inactivity limits independently per channel type (session, x11-connection, direct-tcpip) [5], [9]. Client ssh_config supports only ChannelTimeout; UnusedConnectionTimeout is server-only and causes fatal client parser failure [5]. Syntax requires space-separated parameters [5].

Key Evidence: ChannelTimeout in ssh_config accepts space-separated type=interval pairs [5]. UnusedConnectionTimeout terminates connections without active channels on sshd only [9]; using it on client causes fatal error [5].
Implications: Client hardening must utilize ChannelTimeout for automated closing of idle port-forwarding tunnels and X11 sessions, omitting UnusedConnectionTimeout from client configurations.

Security hardening includes defense against traffic analysis side-channels. ObscureKeystrokeTiming (OpenSSH 9.5+, refined in 10.0+) quantizes packet dispatch to 20ms boundaries with chaff packets to prevent keystroke reconstruction [1], [5]. MitM defense relies on StrictHostKeyChecking ask and VerifyHostKeyDNS yes via DNSSEC [5], [8]. Agent isolation is enforced via ForwardAgent no and IdentitiesOnly yes [5], [8].

Key Evidence: ObscureKeystrokeTiming algorithm is detailed in OpenBSD documentation [5]. OpenSSH 10.0 introduced optimizations preventing performance degradation when X11 graphics activity occurs [1].
Mozilla Hardening Guidelines mandate IdentitiesOnly yes to prevent key enumeration and 'Too many authentication failures' [8]. UpdateHostKeys ask facilitates seamless host key rotation [5].
Implications: Deploying ObscureKeystrokeTiming, VerifyHostKeyDNS, IdentitiesOnly, and hardware-backed agent routing provides layered protection across transport and application tiers.
